why-workbooks.q: According to the lesson, what is the new skill that lets a non-coder build software?
options: Saying what you want and judging what comes back
Learning enough syntax to read the agent's code
Memorizing the names of common frameworks and tools
Configuring servers and budgets before you begin
why-workbooks.explain: The lesson says you cross the gap by getting good at saying what you want and judging the result, not by becoming an engineer.

why-workbooks.q: The lesson describes Workbooks not as one product but as what?
options: A subscription service that hosts your finished apps
An ecosystem: a way to hold software, an engine, and agents
A programming language designed for plain-English input
A single app you log into to manage your projects
why-workbooks.explain: It states Workbooks isn't one product you adopt but an ecosystem: a way to hold software, an engine to run it, and agents that build.

why-workbooks.q: What is the lesson's answer to an organization's fear of letting AI touch real systems?
options: Trust the agent because modern models rarely make errors
Keep a human watching every single command the agent runs
The agent runs in a sandbox you own, with revocable powers
Limit the agent to reading data and never writing anything
why-workbooks.explain: The bet is the opposite of trusting the agent: it runs inside a sandbox you own with deliberate, revocable powers and secrets kept off the computer.

why-workbooks.q: Why does the lesson call this 'the durable shape' rather than just an AI tool?
options: Because the agents improve faster than any rival product
Because a company guarantees it will support the format forever
Because it hides its complexity behind a polished interface
Because it's built on standards that outlived a dozen trends
why-workbooks.explain: It's steadier than an AI tool because every part rests on lasting standards: an ordinary file, a plain format, an engine you can run yourself.

why-workbooks.q: For a team, what is the 'quiet idea' underneath Workbooks?
options: Work can travel as one thing that explains itself on arrival
Every tool a team uses should be replaced by a single vendor
Slack threads should be the permanent record of every decision
Teams should grant the agent access to all six of their services
why-workbooks.explain: The idea is that a piece of work, its screen, data, and history can travel as one thing you hand off, explaining itself on arrival.

tell-it-what-you-want.q: The lesson says the most important skill for a first request is what?
options: Knowing a programming language well enough to check work
Writing a complete, flawless spec before you ever send it
Asking well: saying clearly what you want a capable builder to do
Spelling out the exact steps the agent should follow
tell-it-what-you-want.explain: It frames the key skill as the old human skill of asking well, saying what you want clearly enough that someone capable can do it.

tell-it-what-you-want.q: Why is the to-do-list request better than the flexbox-and-divs request?
options: It is far longer and lists more technical requirements
It tells the agent exactly which sorting function to write
It names a popular layout the agent should always prefer
It describes the outcome, so the agent can pick a better road
tell-it-what-you-want.explain: The second is shorter and better because it gives purpose, audience, and feel, letting the agent choose a better construction than you'd spell out.

tell-it-what-you-want.q: Which of these does the lesson present as a key thing a first request should include?
options: How you'll know it worked, a finish line you can check
A list of the specific files the agent should create
The framework and database the agent ought to choose
A guess at the layout so the agent doesn't have to decide
tell-it-what-you-want.explain: The four things a new colleague would need include 'how will you know it worked' — a finish line the agent can aim at and you can check.

tell-it-what-you-want.q: What rule does the lesson tell you to carry away about quality?
options: Magic phrasing matters more than the detail you provide
Vague in, vague out; specific in, specific out
Always keep requests as short as possibly can be
Technical wording produces a more specific result
tell-it-what-you-want.explain: The rule is 'vague in, vague out; specific in, specific out' — detail about the outcome is the biggest lever on result quality.

tell-it-what-you-want.q: What does the lesson mean when it says 'specific does not mean technical'?
options: You should add code only after the first draft comes back
Technical detail is fine as long as it's also very specific
Rich, specific description of the outcome can use no code at all
Specific requests must name at least one piece of technology
tell-it-what-you-want.explain: The better dog-walking request had not one word of code; being richly specific about the outcome while staying out of construction is the move.

the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.q: What does the lesson say experienced people actually have that beginners lack?
options: A secret set of magic words that produce perfect output
The ability to read and fix the agent's code themselves
A better, more detailed first prompt than everyone else
A loop they trust: say it, look hard, say the next thing
the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.explain: There are no magic words; experienced people have a loop they trust — say what they want, look hard, redirect — run over and over.

the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.q: What are the three beats of the loop, in order?
options: Prompt, Look, Redirect
Plan, Build, Deploy
Describe, Wait, Accept
Ask, Approve, Repeat
the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.explain: The loop has three beats run in order: Prompt (say what you want), Look (examine what came back), Redirect (name what's off).

the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.q: Which beat does the lesson warn people most often skip, causing projects to go wrong?
options: The prompt, because people overthink the wording
The look, actually examining whether it's really right
The redirect, because corrections feel confrontational
The restart, because people refuse to begin again
the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.explain: Look is the beat people skip — actually examining whether it is right, not whether it sounds right — and skipping it is where projects go wrong.

the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.q: In the pottery-workshop example, what made the redirect effective?
options: It re-explained the entire project from the beginning
It told the agent to make the whole thing better overall
It named exactly what was seen: a notes box and remaining spots
It started over rather than building on the prior version
the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.explain: The redirect worked because it named the specific results seen — add a notes box, show remaining spots — giving the agent concrete targets.

the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.q: Why does the lesson say it's safe to run a tight loop fast?
options: Because the agent rarely makes a wrong turn in practice
Because a human approves each change before it is saved
Because bold redirects are tested in a separate copy first
Because the workbook records its history, so you can undo
the-loop-prompt-look-redirect.explain: It's safe because a workbook keeps its own history with a way back, so the cost of a bad lap is just one more lap.

reading-what-it-did.q: What mindset does the lesson recommend taking toward the agent?
options: A talented, fast, slightly overconfident colleague to verify
An infallible oracle whose output you can safely accept
An enemy that is probably trying to deceive you each time
A junior who needs every step spelled out in advance
reading-what-it-did.explain: Treat the agent as a talented, fast, slightly overconfident colleague on their first week — verify the work rather than assume it.

reading-what-it-did.q: Why does the lesson call 'it looks fine' a coin flip?
options: Because skimming takes longer than a proper review does
Because confident fiction and wrong-thing-done-well look correct
Because the agent always hides its mistakes deliberately
Because reading the agent's description is enough to be sure
reading-what-it-did.explain: Two mistakes sail through a skim — confident fiction and doing the wrong thing well — because both produce output that looks like correct work.

reading-what-it-did.q: What is 'drift' as the lesson defines it?
options: The agent slowing down as a project grows larger
A dramatic failure where the agent crashes mid-task
Slowly solving a slightly different problem than yours
The agent forgetting earlier parts of the conversation
reading-what-it-did.explain: Drift is the agent slowly solving a slightly different problem than the one you have, accumulating small wrong turns that each looked reasonable.

reading-what-it-did.q: What makes the ledger a record the agent 'can't fake'?
options: The agent reviews and signs the log before it is sealed
A second agent rewrites the log to confirm it is honest
The agent chooses which steps are important enough to record
The system writes each action at a chokepoint, then seals it
reading-what-it-did.explain: The agent doesn't hold the pen; the system records every action at a chokepoint and seals the log, so any later edit breaks the stamp.

reading-what-it-did.q: What does the lesson say the best evals are?
options: Traps that plant the exact mistake this task tends to make
Checklists that confirm every feature is present and working
Final-answer graders that read only the agent's conclusion
One-time reviews you run by hand on each individual change
reading-what-it-did.explain: The best evals aren't checklists, they're traps: you plant the exact mistake the task tends to make, and a pass means the agent didn't bite.

first-workbook-end-to-end.q: What is the whole skill Dana brings, according to the lesson?
options: A little hidden coding ability she rarely admits to
Describing clearly what she wants, like briefing a new hire
Knowing which framework and database to choose up front
Reading the agent's code closely to catch its errors
first-workbook-end-to-end.explain: Dana can't code; her whole skill is describing what she wants clearly, the way she'd brief a sharp new hire.

first-workbook-end-to-end.q: What did the agent do after reading Dana's first brief?
options: Silently guessed at the unclear parts and built immediately
Returned a wall of code for Dana to review line by line
Asked two decisions that change the result: live-update and dropdowns
Refused to start until Dana provided a complete spec
first-workbook-end-to-end.explain: The agent showed up as a collaborator, finding the two decisions that change the result — live updates and dropdown vs. free text — and asking.

first-workbook-end-to-end.q: When Dana reviews the tool, what is she actually judging?
options: The quality and structure of the underlying code
Whether the agent's description sounds accurate
How fast the agent finished the build
The result against what she asked for, like any draft
first-workbook-end-to-end.explain: Dana doesn't read code; she reviews the result against what she asked for, and is more qualified than the agent because she knows her team.

first-workbook-end-to-end.q: What are the 'three levels' the lesson names for the agent?
options: It answers, it checks itself, it works with you over time
It plans, it codes, it deploys without your involvement
It listens, it remembers, it eventually runs on its own
It drafts, it tests, it replaces the human director
first-workbook-end-to-end.explain: The three levels are: Level 1 it answers, Level 2 it checks itself, Level 3 it works with you over time as a collaborator.

first-workbook-end-to-end.q: What does the lesson say about putting Dana's workbook on the web?
options: It requires rebuilding the tool for a different environment
It's closer to flipping one setting than the dreaded deploy
It demands a separate hosting account and a build step
It only works after engineers review the whole project
first-workbook-end-to-end.explain: Going live is closer to flipping one setting than the white-knuckle deploy engineers dread; the same thing runs, just somewhere else.

the-one-file.q: What is the core unit of everything in Workbooks, per the lesson?
options: The runtime server that hosts and scales the projects
The org layer that records the intent and the tasks
A workbook, which at first glance looks like an HTML page
The SQLite database that holds the saved data
the-one-file.explain: The thing you walk away with is a workbook, the core unit; it looks like a web page, an .html file, the format the internet is built on.

the-one-file.q: What does the lesson correct about 'a workbook is just one HTML file'?
options: A workbook is actually a proprietary archive, not HTML
A workbook can't run without being connected to a server
A workbook is only the visible screen, never the data
When it travels it's a small bundle, and the bundle is the unit
the-one-file.explain: The first correction: a workbook is not only a single HTML file; when it travels it's a small bundle, and the bundle is what you own and send.

the-one-file.q: Which four standards are bound into the workbook bundle?
options: HTML, SQLite, org, and a one-line manifest
HTML, JSON, Python, and a config file
HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and a database driver
HTML, zip, Elixir, and a manifest
the-one-file.explain: The bundle binds four standards: workbook.html for the face, vfs.sqlite for the disk, workbook.org for the why, and manifest.json to bind them.

the-one-file.q: What does the lesson identify as the over-claim it wants to retire?
options: That a workbook is a plain zip you can open with unzip
That single workbooks can open and run on their own
That a workbook is self-contained, so there's no server
That the bundle's formats are boring and openable
the-one-file.explain: The claim to retire is 'no server': a single workbook runs alone, but for agents, other languages, or scale it stands on a runtime.

the-one-file.q: How does the lesson describe the relationship between the file and the runtime?
options: The runtime replaces the file once a project gets large
The file and runtime are two competing ways to ship software
The file is the unit you hold; the runtime is the ground it stands on
The runtime is bundled inside every single workbook file
the-one-file.explain: The workbook is the core unit you hold and hand off; the runtime is the ground it stands on when you want more than a single page.

carries-its-story.q: How does a workbook keep knowing what it is after you rename the file to anything?
options: Its file extension is locked so a rename can never alter the type.
The browser caches the original name and restores it on open.
A hidden magic header in the first bytes declares its true type.
It carries an internal marker block that describes what it is.
carries-its-story.explain: Identity lives inside the file as a marker block, so a rename never reaches it.

carries-its-story.q: What is the filename's one humble remaining job during a library scan?
options: It narrows the pile so the scan need not crack open every file.
It is the only way the tool decides which files are workbooks.
It stores the workbook's embedded source for fast retrieval later.
It records the author and timestamp of the most recent change.
carries-its-story.explain: The extension narrows the haystack for economy, but the marker is still the needle.

carries-its-story.q: Why can a workbook carry its own source while still looking like one finished thing?
options: The browser compiles the source on load and discards the original text.
The readable source folds into a second inert block the browser ignores.
The source is fetched from a server the moment someone unpacks the file.
A binary section stores the recipe in a sealed, unreadable container.
carries-its-story.explain: The human-written source rides along in a second inert block the browser leaves untouched.

carries-its-story.q: How does a workbook project keep its history instead of scattering it?
options: It uploads every revision to a vendor dashboard's activity log.
It saves periodic snapshots in a separate folder beside the files.
Its working space is a version-controlled repository kept inside it.
It records only the final published version and discards the rest.
carries-its-story.explain: The project's working space is a version-controlled repo, so history travels with it.

carries-its-story.q: What makes the author of each recorded change trustworthy rather than a typed label?
options: The name is verified against a central company directory at publish time.
Each change requires a fresh password confirming the author manually.
The author field is locked once written and can never be edited again.
A real cryptographic identity backs the name and survives a wipe.
carries-its-story.explain: Authorship rests on a portable cryptographic identity, not a name typed into a field.

the-one-language.q: What is the central claim this lesson makes about what an agent writes?
options: The material underneath is just readable plain text you can check.
The agent hides its real plan in a private machine language.
Only experts trained on the tooling can decode what was written.
The running result is all there is; nothing underlies it.
the-one-language.explain: The whole idea is that the layer you and the agent stand on is just readable.

the-one-language.q: What trade do the two usual ways of writing software's story force on you?
options: You must pick a vendor's format and stay locked inside its tools.
You get prose or structure in one place, never both together.
You choose between speed and accuracy when the machine parses it.
You sacrifice readability for a smaller file that loads faster.
the-one-language.explain: Pretty prose is meaningless to a machine; tidy structure has no room for human thought.

the-one-language.q: Where did the org convention come from?
options: It was invented fresh for this project to unify its layers.
It is a proprietary dialect owned by a single vendor.
It is a roughly twenty-year-old convention for plain-text notes.
It is a rebranding of HTML extended to describe meaning.
the-one-language.explain: Org is a ~20-year-old open convention for notes, to-dos, and schedules, not newly invented.

the-one-language.q: What does org's readability actually give you about agent drift?
options: It prevents an agent from ever repeating or contradicting itself.
It compresses the text so contradictions cannot fit in the file.
It locks the document so only the host can change a line.
It makes drift catchable, since a checker can walk it and notice.
the-one-language.explain: Org doesn't prevent drift; being machine-readable makes the drift catchable instead of hidden.

the-one-language.q: Why does learning to read one format let you read every corner of a project?
options: The same org grammar shows up in intent, manuals, deploys, and plans.
A translator converts each part into your preferred file format.
Every part is rewritten into prose whenever you open it.
Each layer uses its own dialect that the reader auto-detects.
the-one-language.explain: The same readable grammar appears everywhere, so you learn it once and read it all.

coming-alive.q: What changes when a workbook on your laptop comes alive?
options: The file is rewritten into a server-specific binary format.
Nothing about the file changes; the thing it stands on does.
The browser injects new code so the page can run on its own.
Its source is stripped out to make room for live state.
coming-alive.explain: The same byte-for-byte file comes alive because of what it stands on, not any file change.

coming-alive.q: What is the Nexus in this system?
options: A file format you hand around like any other workbook.
A cloud-only subscription metered per request you make.
The engine — a place you run that workbooks are set down on.
A converter that exports a workbook into a deployable app.
coming-alive.explain: The Nexus is the load-bearing engine, a place you stand on, not a file you carry.

coming-alive.q: How do the three words Nexus, dock, and the Dock relate?
options: They are three separate systems you configure independently.
They are older names for one deprecated deployment step.
They describe three competing engines you pick between.
One motion seen three ways: the place, the act, the doorway.
coming-alive.explain: Nexus is the place, to dock is the act, the Dock is the doorway between them.

coming-alive.q: Which trio of lights switches on when you dock a workbook?
options: Isolated, stateful, and agentic.
Compiled, encrypted, and signed.
Cached, indexed, and replicated.
Public, billed, and metered.
coming-alive.explain: Docking flips three lights at once: isolated, stateful, and agentic.

coming-alive.q: Why can one ordinary machine carry many workbooks at once?
options: Each workbook is paused unless someone is actively viewing it.
The BEAM juggles huge numbers of tiny isolated processes.
Workbooks share one process so overhead stays near zero.
The engine rents extra virtual machines per workbook by the second.
coming-alive.explain: The BEAM was built to juggle vast numbers of lightweight, isolated processes.

why-a-sandbox.q: What are the two things that actually go wrong with an agent doing real work?
options: It runs too slowly and it forgets earlier parts of the task.
It writes buggy code and it picks the wrong AI model.
It reaches where it shouldn't, and it gets hijacked through the work.
It costs too much per run and it crashes the host machine.
why-a-sandbox.explain: The two nightmares are excess reach and prompt injection riding in on the work.

why-a-sandbox.q: How does a sandbox differ from putting a guard in front of your secrets?
options: It checks permissions twice instead of once before each action.
It encrypts the secrets so a guard can't read them if fooled.
It logs every access so a fooled guard can be caught later.
It builds a room that doesn't contain the secrets at all.
why-a-sandbox.explain: There's no door to guard because the secrets were never in the agent's room.

why-a-sandbox.q: What does the phrase "grant the verb, keep the noun" mean here?
options: The agent gets the ability to act, never the dangerous thing itself.
The agent is given verbs to log but nouns to execute directly.
The host renames secrets so the agent can't recognize them.
The agent may read keys but is forbidden from sending them.
why-a-sandbox.explain: The agent gets the ability to sign or fetch, never the key or network that's dangerous.

why-a-sandbox.q: What's the difference between "forbidden" and "doesn't exist" for a capability?
options: Forbidden means slower access; doesn't exist means no access at all.
Forbidden has a check that can fail; doesn't exist has nothing to check.
Forbidden applies to data; doesn't exist applies only to networks.
Forbidden is temporary; doesn't exist means revoked for this run.
why-a-sandbox.explain: A forbidden capability still exists and is checked; an absent one has nothing to check.

why-a-sandbox.q: Which wall in the sandbox is described as the most thoroughly tested?
options: The memory limit, pinned down by a dedicated automated suite.
The file-system wall, verified by checks after a past leak.
The network wall, pinned by checks after an early leak was caught.
The shell wall, proven by repeated red-team attempts.
why-a-sandbox.explain: The network wall is the most tested, pinned by checks after an early version leaked.

safe-powers.q: What is the narrower, more honest claim this lesson actually makes?
options: Every dangerous power is silently filtered before it can run.
The powers are removed entirely so nothing risky remains.
A smarter guard catches every misuse before it happens.
You hand powers over deliberately and can take any back.
safe-powers.explain: The claim is deliberate, named, revocable grants, not danger magically erased.

safe-powers.q: What happens when a workbook reaches for a power it was never granted?
options: It fails to even start, because it asked for a tool never wired in.
It gets a quiet "no" and continues with reduced abilities.
It pauses and prompts the host to grant the power on demand.
It logs the attempt and silently skips that one action.
safe-powers.explain: An ungranted power doesn't exist, so the workbook fails to start rather than being denied.

safe-powers.q: What does the minimal profile actually include?
options: Only a disk and nothing else, a fully sealed scratch space.
Disk, commands, storage, a queue, plus secrets and brokered sockets.
Everything except the ability to call a language model.
Outbound web and browsing but no local disk or storage.
safe-powers.explain: Minimal is a working surface that also grants secrets and brokered sockets, not a sealed space.

safe-powers.q: What happens if someone names a profile that doesn't exist, like a typo?
options: It grants the network rung so the run isn't blocked.
It refuses to run until a valid profile name is supplied.
It falls closed to the pure-compute floor, disk and nothing else.
It inherits the last profile that successfully ran before it.
safe-powers.explain: Unknown profiles fall closed to the most restrictive disk-only floor, pinned by a test.

safe-powers.q: How can a workbook use a secret without ever being able to leak it?
options: The secret is encrypted inside the workbook and decrypted on use.
The workbook reads the key but is audited every time it does.
The host rotates the key fast enough that a leak goes stale.
It names and uses the secret but never reads it; the host signs.
safe-powers.explain: With secrets granted it can name and use a secret but never read it; the host holds the key.

going-live.q: Why is going live usually terrifying, according to the lesson?
options: Many separate services must all agree at once for the move to work.
The new place runs different code than your local prototype did.
Deploying always erases your data unless you back it up first.
The cloud charges unpredictable fees the moment you publish.
going-live.explain: The fear is the committee of services that must all line up, not the new place itself.

going-live.q: What is a deployment, in this system's terms?
options: A scripted sequence of steps that must run in the right order.
A short list of five decisions the engine converges reality to.
A configuration file packed with hooks and embedded commands.
A one-time export that bakes the current state into a binary.
going-live.explain: A deployment is five decisions described as an end state the engine converges to.

going-live.q: What does the validation check do before letting you go live?
options: It starts a test machine to confirm the deploy actually boots.
It rewrites the config to fix problems for you automatically.
It refuses configurations that would quietly betray you, read-only.
It flags style issues so the file reads more cleanly.
going-live.explain: The read-only check refuses lying configs, like many tenants with single-user storage.

going-live.q: What does the public /_changes endpoint serve, and how?
options: A full admin console gated behind a required login.
A live edit surface where anyone can push new commits.
The secrets and build tools, available only to authorized users.
The history feed, anonymous and read-only, newest first.
going-live.explain: /_changes is an anonymous, read-only GET serving recent changes and agent status.

going-live.q: How does moving from your laptop to production actually work?
options: You change one setting; local and cloud are values of one axis.
You rebuild the app for the cloud's different engine and runtime.
You migrate through a separate deploy pipeline and rebuild train.
You re-author the prototype into a production-grade version.
going-live.explain: Local and cloud are two values of one setting; the same engine and bytes run on both.

giving-it-abilities.q: What does an agent reach for when it needs an ability it doesn't have?
options: A plugin locked to whichever platform supplied it.
A toolkit: one packaged ability it can find, learn, and run safely.
A raw package installed onto your machine at your own risk.
A custom protocol bolted onto the agent for each new tool.
giving-it-abilities.explain: An agent reaches for a toolkit, one packaged ability bundled to be found and run safely.

giving-it-abilities.q: What three things does a toolkit bundle into one object?
options: A license key, a price, and a support contract.
A network protocol, a server, and a registry entry.
The program, the manual, and the sandbox wrapper.
A display name, an icon, and a version number.
giving-it-abilities.explain: A toolkit ships code, manual, and the sandbox wrapper bound together as one object.

giving-it-abilities.q: How is a toolkit's "muscle" layer built?
options: A fresh program written from scratch for every new toolkit.
A description of a program the agent interprets at run time.
A cloud service the toolkit calls out to over the network.
A real program compiled into the portable form browsers run.
giving-it-abilities.explain: The muscle is a real program brought across into the portable form that runs in browsers.

giving-it-abilities.q: Why can the manual double as the agent's instructions for the tool?
options: It is structured text precise enough to be how the tool is reached.
A separate hidden spec is generated from it for the agent to read.
The agent rewrites the loose prose into commands before each use.
The manual is compiled into the program so they never diverge.
giving-it-abilities.explain: Structured manual text is precise enough to reach the tool, so docs can't drift from it.

giving-it-abilities.q: How does the shared collection of toolkits actually grow?
options: A central team writes and approves each new toolkit in advance.
Useful things built inside workbooks get promoted into toolkits.
Vendors submit toolkits to an app store for paid distribution.
The engine auto-generates toolkits from popular agent requests.
giving-it-abilities.explain: Build something useful inside a workbook and one step promotes it into a shared toolkit.

code-in-the-document.q: What core problem does writing the system as one document solve?
options: It makes the running code faster to compile and ship
It lets one team own the code and another own the docs
It stops the description and the running system from drifting apart
It replaces every config language with a single new format
code-in-the-document.explain: The document IS the software, so what is written and what runs can never quietly disagree.

code-in-the-document.q: Where do a component's connections to other components actually live?
options: Inside the source code block of each component
In a separate wiring diagram kept beside the document
In a config file the orchestrator reads at startup
In short tags on the line where the code begins
code-in-the-document.explain: Connections live in the prose layer as plain labels, not inside the code itself.

code-in-the-document.q: How does the function that places a component figure out its structure?
options: From the short surface tags, never reading the code inside
By compiling and tracing each component's actual code
By asking the author to draw the wiring by hand
By inspecting which language each block is written in
code-in-the-document.explain: It works entirely from the surface tags and never reads the code inside a component.

code-in-the-document.q: How does a connection between two components get created?
options: A developer draws a line between them in the editor
An output label and a matching input label meet
The compiler infers it from the shared programming language
The scheduler pairs them by their run order at runtime
code-in-the-document.explain: A producer of a list of events meets a consumer of that list, and the connection appears from the labels.

code-in-the-document.q: What kind of error can the plan validate before any code is compiled?
options: A component whose code will throw at runtime later
A permission grant that the host will refuse to honor
A dangling input wired to nothing that produces it
A language mismatch between two connected components
code-in-the-document.explain: An input asking for a list nothing produces is caught and named as an error before compilation.

the-one-command.q: Who is the primary operator of work in your workflow?
options: You, typing each verb yourself at the terminal
A separate machine-only service you never see
The host engine, which owns all the cleverness
Your agent, which types the commands for you
the-one-command.explain: When you ask the agent to scaffold, wire, or ship, the agent is the one typing work commands.

the-one-command.q: What is the honest description of what work actually is?
options: A handle, not a brain, that hands heavy work to the engine
A self-contained brain holding all the build intelligence
A getting-started tutorial you run for two minutes
A machine-only protocol with no human-facing side
the-one-command.explain: It parses the request, does light local work, and hands everything heavy to the engine behind it.

the-one-command.q: How does work behave differently for machines versus people?
options: It runs entirely different code paths for each kind of user
It drops menus and colors for clean, predictable output
It refuses to run at all unless a human is at the terminal
It splits into two separate programs that share no source
the-one-command.explain: For machines it drops friendliness for clean output and stable codes; the work underneath stays the same.

the-one-command.q: What is special about where work runs?
options: It exists only as a laptop install for three platforms
It runs as a translated stand-in inside the engine
The very same tool runs inside the engine's sandbox
It is recompiled into a different tool for the engine
the-one-command.explain: The same work a person installs runs inside the sandbox, so people and AI hold the identical tool.

the-one-command.q: What is the job of the doctor verb?
options: It repairs a broken workbook by rewriting its source
It installs missing compilers and toolkits automatically
It signs a workbook so its origin travels with it
It checks setup and reports findings without failing the shell
the-one-command.explain: doctor runs honest probes, reports in plain language, and never fails the shell just for finding a problem.

what-an-agent-is.q: What is the complete definition of an agent in this lesson?
options: A model, in a loop, with tools
A planner driving a graph of tasks
A digital employee that decides everything
A database of memory bolted onto a model
what-an-agent-is.explain: The whole thing is stated plainly: an agent is a model, in a loop, with tools.

what-an-agent-is.q: What does the loop actually consist of?
options: A planner assigning steps to worker processes
Reading, acting, looking at the result, repeating
A graph engine resolving dependencies in order
A hidden mind deciding actions behind a curtain
what-an-agent-is.explain: The model reads, picks an action, reads the result, and circles again until the work is done.

what-an-agent-is.q: How many built-in hands does an agent get in this ecosystem?
options: None, since the model only ever produces words
One per toolkit, wired in for each new ability
Exactly one: a shell, the same as a person would use
As many as the plugins and protocols it loads
what-an-agent-is.explain: An agent gets exactly one hand, a shell, and every other capability comes through toolkits.

what-an-agent-is.q: What is the mental shift the lesson urges for agents?
options: From shell commands to specialized plugin wiring
From a single chat to a long sequence of chats
From cheap fast models to expensive careful ones
From conversation to tenure, a worker given a place
what-an-agent-is.explain: You stop summoning an agent for an answer and instead give it a workspace and a rhythm over time.

what-an-agent-is.q: What is the honest framing the lesson insists on?
options: People and AI building together, with direction staying human
Software that finally runs itself without you
An autopilot that makes the operator optional
An agent that grabs whatever powers it decides it needs
what-an-agent-is.explain: The pitch is never self-running software; the loop gets work done but does not make you optional.

agents-that-persist.q: What simple trick makes an agent persistent across long work?
options: Holding one connection open for the whole job
Splitting the request apart from the work itself
Storing every transcript in a large database
Running the model faster so it finishes in seconds
agents-that-persist.explain: When you start a run you get an immediate receipt; the work lives elsewhere so you can walk away.

agents-that-persist.q: What is the receptionist's job in a persistent run?
options: Calling the model and running the agent's tools
Thinking through the hardest step of the task
Staying reachable and answering status instantly
Deciding when the run should stop and ask a human
agents-that-persist.explain: The receptionist stays reachable and answers status immediately, even while the worker is busy.

agents-that-persist.q: What is true about standing agents versus a run you start by hand?
options: They use a fancier engine reserved for schedules
They cannot be started manually, only on a timer
They skip the receptionist and worker split entirely
They run the exact same engine, just a different door
agents-that-persist.explain: There is one engine with two front doors; the scheduled agent does the same work the same way.

agents-that-persist.q: How do persistent agents avoid costing a fortune when idle?
options: They stretch the gap longer after each idle wake-up
They shut down permanently after the first empty run
They switch to a cheaper model whenever idle
They hand idle work off to the receptionist instead
agents-that-persist.explain: After an idle wake-up the system waits longer before the next, stretching the gaps until work returns.

agents-that-persist.q: How does a persistent run get a human decision when it needs one?
options: It guesses and proceeds, logging the choice for review
It pauses, opens a door by its name, and waits for you
It cancels the run and asks you to start over
It escalates to another agent to make the call
agents-that-persist.explain: Because a run knows its name, it stops, hands you the question, and holds its place until you answer.

did-it-do-well.q: Why does skimming a transcript fail as a quality check?
options: Transcripts are too long to ever finish reading
The agent hides its real output from the reader
Dangerous failures read like correct, fluent prose
The model deletes the steps that went wrong
did-it-do-well.explain: Following injected instructions or making things up both come out as fluent prose that looks right.

did-it-do-well.q: What two parts make up an eval?
options: A model and a loop that runs it repeatedly
A receptionist and a worker grading the run
A unit test and a structural wiring check
A brief (the task) and a rubric (the standard)
did-it-do-well.explain: An eval bundles a brief and a rubric, run against the live agent and judged pass or fail.

did-it-do-well.q: What does the judge get to see beyond the agent's final answer?
options: The path: steps taken, tools used, and errors
The source code of the agent being graded
The author's private notes about the rubric
A second judge's verdict on the same run
did-it-do-well.explain: The harness reads the logged record and writes step count, tools used, and error count into the judge's prompt.

did-it-do-well.q: What makes a strong rubric different from a weak one?
options: It restates the task and asks if it was answered
It uses a more expensive judge model to decide
It names how this agent fails and sets a trap
It checks whether the output loads and is wired up
did-it-do-well.explain: A strong rubric names the specific failure mode and makes pass mean the agent didn't take the bait.

did-it-do-well.q: What should you do when a stage fails on its first eval run?
options: Rerun it until the flaky verdict turns green
Switch to a cheaper judge to save on cost
Treat the failure as signal that the agent is wrong
Add more rubrics until one of them passes
did-it-do-well.explain: A failing bench is signal; tuning the test until it passes is lying to yourself with extra steps.

plans-that-run.q: What is the stubborn idea a workbook plan rests on?
options: The plan should live in a dedicated tracker app
The plan needs a separate database for its cards
The plan is a note that summarizes the real work
The plan is the work, not a note about the work
plans-that-run.explain: Instead of a note beside the work, the plan IS the work, written as the only copy in one file.

plans-that-run.q: What does it mean for a task to be ready?
options: It is unfinished and everything it depends on is done
It has been assigned a priority by the scheduler
It has reached its declared timestamp on the calendar
A human has dragged its card into the doing column
plans-that-run.explain: Ready means unfinished plus all dependencies done; that single fact runs the whole loop.

plans-that-run.q: How is the kanban board related to the plan file?
options: It is stored in its own table with a column schema
It is a two-way rendering that reads and writes the file
It is a read-only screenshot drawn once at deploy
It is a separate tracker that mirrors the work
plans-that-run.explain: The board has a read half drawing columns and a write half flipping the word back in the same file.

plans-that-run.q: How does a scheduled task actually fire at its declared time?
options: The text file animates itself when the clock matches
A notification system pushes the task at the timestamp
An engine-side heartbeat wakes the agent to read the plan
The board polls the calendar and triggers the run
plans-that-run.explain: The declared timestamp is for reading; a steady engine heartbeat wakes the agent to notice what's due.

plans-that-run.q: What does running a plan honestly NOT promise?
options: That a stuck task will always have a nameable cause
That contradictions in the plan become catchable facts
That a person and an agent can clear the same list
That the plan runs itself without any human direction
plans-that-run.explain: Direction stays human; what changes is that following through gets cheap, not that judgment disappears.

compiled-plans.q: What is the central claim about a plan written for human eyes?
options: That plan itself can be the running system
That plan must be translated into code first
That plan is a spec handed to an engineer
That plan is only a diagram of the work
compiled-plans.explain: The same steps, order, and dependencies you'd naturally describe are what executes; there is no second artifact.

compiled-plans.q: Where does the running order of steps come from?
options: From a configuration of runners and pools you set
From the dependencies you naturally describe
From a hand-written table of step priorities
From the order the steps appear in the file
compiled-plans.explain: The dependencies you describe are already the schedule; the engine peels the plan into ready layers.

compiled-plans.q: What is the deliberate limit on how steps take input?
options: A step may hand its result to at most one other step
A step must depend on every earlier step in the plan
Each step takes at most one input from upstream
Each step must combine two upstream results at once
compiled-plans.explain: Each step takes at most one input; joining two streams must be done by an upstream step producing the combined thing.

compiled-plans.q: How do you get two agents running in parallel in a plan?
options: Flip a parallelism setting on each agent step
Mark both steps as agents and chain them together
Assign them to two different runner pools
Give the two agent steps no dependency on each other
compiled-plans.explain: Parallelism is the absence of a dependency; with no link the steps land in the same layer and run together.

compiled-plans.q: What is the one-directional safety rule for changing a deployed plan?
options: What you give may grow but never shrink; demands may shrink not grow
What you give may shrink but never grow; demands may grow not shrink
Both what you give and what you demand may only grow
Both what you give and what you demand may only shrink
compiled-plans.explain: Removing an output may break downstream readers; asking for more capability may exceed what the host grants.

options: A new kind of engine that rewrites its own deep machinery over time
A standing agent working a maintenance plan, aimed at the system itself
A chat window where you ask the system to fix problems on demand
A separate model trained only to detect bugs in shipped software
the-system-improves-itself.explain: The autopoet is just an agent and a plan pointed inward at the system.

the-system-improves-itself.q: What layer is the autopoet allowed to change?
options: The running engine, but only after a full reboot completes
Any code, as long as the change passes the verify gates first
The declarative layer of plain text: tools, skills, docs, job descriptions
The compiled binaries, since plain text would be too slow to edit
the-system-improves-itself.explain: It edits only the declarative, plain-text layer; the engine is fixed.

the-system-improves-itself.q: How does the autopoet learn what needs fixing?
options: It scans live performance data and forecasts problems on its own
A human reopens the project and assigns it a list of fixes
It reboots agents periodically and watches which ones fail
Working agents file tickets when their own tools fall short
the-system-improves-itself.explain: Working agents notice tool gaps and file tickets the autopoet reads.

the-system-improves-itself.q: Why is 'software that edits itself' safe here?
options: Every change is a reviewable text diff that runs the same gates
The autopoet is trusted, so its changes skip the usual checks
Changes apply only after a human approves each one by hand
The engine quietly reboots to undo anything that goes wrong
the-system-improves-itself.explain: Changes are reviewable, revertible text diffs facing the normal gates.

the-system-improves-itself.q: What is true about the autopoet today?
options: It already reads live performance data and improves with no prompting
Phase 1, the issue backlog, is built and running on this project
It can edit the engine as long as the change is well documented
It is purely a planned idea with nothing actually shipped yet
the-system-improves-itself.explain: Phase 1, the ticket backlog, is real; the self-reading bet is unfinished.

proving-origin.q: Where does a workbook's proof of origin have to live?
options: On a registry server that anyone can query to confirm it
In a separate signature file shipped alongside the workbook
Inside the file itself, surviving a byte-for-byte copy
On the platform the workbook was originally published from
proving-origin.explain: The proof must ride inside the artifact so it survives copying offline.

proving-origin.q: How does the signer's identity work in the seal?
options: It is a name that points at a key stored on a server
It is a certificate fetched from a trusted authority on check
It is a username registered in the platform's account system
The identity string is itself the signer's public verifying key
proving-origin.explain: The identity is the key written out, so nothing needs looking up.

proving-origin.q: Why does verifying a signed workbook ask two questions?
options: To separate whether the seal is genuine from whether bytes changed
To check the signer's name against a master list of trusted authors
To confirm both the timestamp and the network connection are valid
To compare the file against the original copy stored on the server
proving-origin.explain: One question checks the signature, the other checks the bytes unchanged.

proving-origin.q: How is the self-referencing fingerprint problem solved?
options: The seal is stored in a second file so the bytes never move
Fingerprint the page as if the seal weren't there, stripping it first
The fingerprint is recomputed and re-signed until the bytes settle
Only the seal block is fingerprinted, never the rest of the page
proving-origin.explain: Strip any seal, fingerprint what remains, so adding it back can't spoil it.

proving-origin.q: What does a valid seal actually prove?
options: That the workbook's contents are trustworthy and safe to run
That a trusted authority has vouched for the signer's real name
The bytes are untouched since signing, by the holder of this key
That the signing timestamp was witnessed by a neutral clock
proving-origin.explain: It proves continuity under a claimed key, not trustworthiness or true name.

who-sees-what.q: Why is a password box inside a single file not real protection?
options: The password is too short for browsers to check it securely
The file forgets the password whenever it is forwarded by email
The check only works while the original server stays online
The file carries both the lock and the data, readable via view source
who-sees-what.explain: A single file ships the guard with the treasure; you can read past it.

who-sees-what.q: What is the real rule for keeping a secret out of the wrong hands?
options: Keep the secret out of the file entirely, not hidden or encrypted in it
Encrypt the secret strongly enough that no one can decrypt it
Hide the secret in a part of the file most readers won't open
Ask the program to refuse access to the secret on load
who-sees-what.explain: The only way to guard a secret is to keep it out of the file.

who-sees-what.q: Which stance means the shell is public but the data isn't in the file?
options: Public, where everything including the data is baked in openly
Gated data, where contents are fetched from a server that checks first
Gated route, where even the app's existence is hidden entirely
Sealed, where the data ships encrypted but travels with the file
who-sees-what.explain: Gated data means a public shell but contents fetched after a check.

who-sees-what.q: When does the system enforce the stance you declared?
options: When someone opens the file, by running a check on page load
When the recipient tries to read the gated data over the wire
When the workbook is being turned into a file, refusing to build
When the file is uploaded, by stripping the secret before sending
who-sees-what.explain: The guard lives at build time; a leaking file is never created.

who-sees-what.q: What does the seal carried inside a workbook claim?
options: That the file is high quality and safe for the recipient to trust
That the contents are hidden from anyone who lacks the key
That a trusted app store has approved the maker's identity
Who stamped it, and that the file hasn't changed a character since
who-sees-what.explain: The seal proves origin and integrity, not goodness and not secrecy.

secrets-in-the-open.q: Why are hidden sheets and scrambled blobs called theater?
options: The holder owns the file and the program, so any check is skippable
They slow the app down enough that users give up reading the data
Browsers refuse to render files that contain encrypted-looking noise
They only work until the original publishing server goes offline
secrets-in-the-open.explain: The holder owns file and program, so any enforced gate is walked through.

secrets-in-the-open.q: What is actually shipped in a sealed section of the file?
options: The plaintext, guarded by a password the program checks on open
Genuine encrypted gibberish, with the key never riding in the file
A link that fetches the real contents from the runtime each time
A scrambled copy that the app unscrambles using a bundled key
secrets-in-the-open.explain: A sealed section is real ciphertext; the key was never shipped at all.

secrets-in-the-open.q: Where is the key, and how is it obtained?
options: Baked into each copy, unlocked once the user enters a password
Stored in the file's metadata, readable only by the original maker
Held at the runtime; a copy asks the engine, which checks who's asking
Cached in the browser after the first successful unlock of the file
secrets-in-the-open.explain: The key lives at the runtime and is released only after an identity check.

secrets-in-the-open.q: How does the design stop a swapped or relabeled section from opening?
options: It logs every key request so misuse can be traced afterward
It checks the section's name against a list of allowed sections
It hides the section names so attackers can't find the right one
Each key is welded to one section, baked into the cryptographic seal
secrets-in-the-open.explain: The section's identity is baked into the seal, so a mismatch won't open.

secrets-in-the-open.q: What is the 'dead-man switch' property of keeping the key home?
options: Delete the one key and every copy everywhere goes dark at once
A remote command reaches out and erases all distributed copies
Each copy self-destructs after a set number of failed unlocks
The runtime tracks copies and revokes them one device at a time
secrets-in-the-open.explain: All copies fetch the same key, so deleting it darkens every copy instantly.

a-disk-that-travels.q: Where does a workbook keep the things its project remembers?
options: In a cloud bucket rented separately for each workbook's data
On its own disk that rides inside the file and travels with it
On the user's real computer, in a folder the workbook controls
In a data center server that the workbook connects to on open
a-disk-that-travels.explain: The disk rides inside the file; it belongs to the project, not a machine.

a-disk-that-travels.q: What lets the disk answer questions a normal disk can't?
options: It runs a background indexer that crawls folders on every open
It connects to a database server whenever a query is needed
Underneath the paths, the disk is built out of database tables
It keeps a separate README cataloging every file by hand
a-disk-that-travels.explain: Built on tables, the disk answers path access and database queries both.

a-disk-that-travels.q: What happens when you unbundle a workbook's disk?
options: It stays locked in an invented format only workbooks can read
It uploads its files to the cloud and leaves a reference behind
It deletes the originals once the copies are safely extracted
It unpacks into ordinary files in ordinary folders on your computer
a-disk-that-travels.explain: The disk unpacks to plain files; the format never holds them hostage.

a-disk-that-travels.q: Why is an agent working inside a workbook's disk safe?
options: Its writing can reach nothing beyond that one project-sized disk
It runs in read-only mode and cannot change any files at all
A human reviews every file the agent writes before it is saved
Its access to your computer is limited to a small scratch folder
a-disk-that-travels.explain: The disk is its whole world, so even a hijacked agent can't reach beyond.

a-disk-that-travels.q: What is the honest limit of a workbook's disk?
options: It cannot store structured data, only loose unorganized files
It is project-scale, meant for megabytes, not a media warehouse
It evaporates the moment you stop paying for the storage meter
It can only be read on the machine that originally created it
a-disk-that-travels.explain: It's project-scale; big freight belongs behind a bigger machine.

the-disk-grows.q: How does a workbook reach live data outside the file?
options: An agent is handed the password and an open connection directly
An export is pasted into the file by hand whenever data is needed
Certain names are registered to point outside, fetched live on ask
The seal is opened so the file can connect to the outside source
the-disk-grows.explain: Registered names fetch live; unregistered names fall through to the file.

the-disk-grows.q: Where does the password for an outside source actually live?
options: Inside the description file that registers the outside name
In the agent's memory, so it can reauthenticate when needed
Baked into each copy of the workbook that needs the data
With the host, which makes the request through one audited path
the-disk-grows.explain: The host holds the credential; the description only names it, never holds it.

the-disk-grows.q: What is the structurally airtight way to give an agent outside data?
options: A background worker pulls data in and writes it to the disk
The agent reaches out itself but only on a gentle schedule
The agent is granted the password for read-only requests only
The agent queries the source live but caches results locally
the-disk-grows.explain: The worker crosses the bridge; the agent only ever reads a local file.

the-disk-grows.q: Why is meaning-based search cheap enough to leave switched on?
options: It calls an outside model fresh for every query a user runs
Meaning is computed once when content is saved, not at search time
It only searches a small summary instead of the real files
It matches exact letters, which is fast but misses meaning
the-disk-grows.explain: Expensive thinking happens on the rare save; searching is a fast lookup.

the-disk-grows.q: How does a workbook move from a local disk to cloud storage?
options: By migrating the code to a vendor's tools threaded through it
By tearing the seal so the program can name the cloud directly
A few lines of configuration outside the program, not code changes
By rewriting each storage call to point at the new backend
the-disk-grows.explain: The code never names where bytes live; configuration swaps the backend.

under-the-hood.q: What reads the grammar across the whole ecosystem?
options: A separate reader for the browser, the CLI, and the server each
A server reader that every other surface calls over the network
A library that each surface configures to its own needs
A single program, the kernel, a small Rust crate of ~500 lines
under-the-hood.explain: One kernel reads the grammar everywhere, so every surface agrees.

under-the-hood.q: What does it mean that the reading core 'has no hands'?
options: It takes text and returns text; it can't touch files or network
It runs only on the server where the operating system guards it
It needs a human to feed it every file it is asked to read
It delegates all reading to toolkits that hold the real powers
under-the-hood.explain: Text in, text out; touching nothing is why it runs everywhere safely.

under-the-hood.q: Why can the renderer, planner, and safety gate be one machine?
options: They share a server that coordinates the three separate tools
They're the same move: read text, understand structure, answer a question
They each load a different copy of the kernel for their own job
They run in sequence, each one feeding its output to the next
under-the-hood.explain: All four jobs are one machine asked different questions about the text.

under-the-hood.q: Why is the reader deliberately built to do so little?
options: To keep it small enough to fit inside a single browser tab
To make it faster than a reader that can touch the disk
Because hands are where danger lives; powerless code is safe anywhere
Because adding powers would require rewriting it for each surface
under-the-hood.explain: A powerless core can't touch disk or network, so it's safe to put anywhere.

under-the-hood.q: Where do new powers come from if the core stays small?
options: From secretly making the reader bigger over each release
From a server tier that lends capabilities to the reader on demand
From the kernel's six functions growing more abilities over time
From toolkits added on the outside, granted deliberately one at a time
under-the-hood.explain: Toolkits add the hands at the edges; the center stays small and trustworthy.

1.q: What does Unit 1 say actually brings down the wall between idea-people and builders?
options: You can describe what you want and an agent builds it
Everyone is finally learning to write code
Servers and compute have gotten far cheaper
Programming languages have grown much simpler
1.explain: The wall falls because you can state an outcome and have a capable agent build it, not because anyone learned to code.

1.q: How does Unit 1 frame what Workbooks is?
options: A single app you sign up for and adopt
An ecosystem of a format, an engine, and agents
A coding course that teaches you the basics
A cloud service that hosts your finished apps
1.explain: Workbooks is framed as an ecosystem, not one product, app, course, or hosting service.

1.q: What is the security bet a worried organization is asked to make?
options: Give the agent full credentials but log everything
Keep all AI strictly offline and air-gapped
The agent runs in a sandbox you own, with revocable powers
Encrypt every file the agent ever touches
1.explain: The bet is the opposite of trusting the agent: it works in a sandbox you own where secrets never touch the machine.

1.q: What does Unit 1 describe a sandbox as?
options: A scheduled backup of your important files
A shared drive your whole team can reach
A code editor with a built-in preview pane
A sealed workspace the agent can't escape from
1.explain: A sandbox is a clean room with the door shut; whatever happens inside can't reach the rest of your machine.

1.q: What single skill does Unit 1 say matters most for the person with an idea?
options: Knowing what good looks like and saying what you want
Writing correct syntax in a chosen language
Setting up and maintaining the infrastructure
Reading the agent's generated code fluently
1.explain: The skill that matters is taste and direction, not syntax, infrastructure, or reading code.

1.q: Why does Unit 1 call this the durable, future-proof shape?
options: It always runs the newest available AI models
It rests on long-lived standards with no proprietary trapdoor
It is backed and guaranteed by a large company
It is consistently the cheapest option on the market
1.explain: It stands on standards that outlived trends, so there is no vendor trapdoor to get locked behind.

2.q: What are the two moving parts of getting something built in Unit 2?
options: You write the code, then you test that code
You describe an outcome, an agent builds it in a sandbox
You pick a template, then you customize its parts
You hire a developer, then you review their work
2.explain: The shape is two parts: you describe what you want, and an agent builds it in a sealed workspace.

2.q: How can a non-coder direct work they can't read line by line?
options: By learning the fundamentals of the code first
By trusting the agent and accepting whatever ships
By judging the result, the way an editor directs a writer
By memorizing the key technical terms involved
2.explain: You direct by judging the result against your goal, not by reading the method, like an editor with a writer.

2.q: What single dial most controls the quality of what you get back?
options: The raw length of the prompt you write
Picking the right underlying technology
The number of revisions you ask for
Specificity about the outcome you want
2.explain: Specificity is the lever: vague in, vague out; specific in, specific out, regardless of length or tech.

2.q: What is the three-beat loop at the heart of Unit 2?
options: Prompt, look, then redirect
Plan, then build, then test
Ask, then accept, then ship
Read, then write, then run
2.explain: The loop run on purpose is prompt, look, redirect; the looking is the beat people skip.

2.q: Which two mistakes slip past a quick skim because they look like real work?
options: A sudden crash and a typo left in the output
Confident fiction and doing the wrong thing well
A slow response time and an ugly page layout
A missing data file and a plainly broken link
2.explain: Both confident fabrication and a well-built wrong thing read as fluent, correct-looking output.

2.q: What is drift, and how does Unit 2 say to handle it?
options: A crash you fix by restarting the agent from scratch
Slow speed you fix by upgrading to better hardware
Slowly solving a slightly different problem; re-anchor
Outdated code you fix by rewriting the whole thing
2.explain: Drift is accumulated small wrong turns; you catch it and re-anchor on the right idea rather than patch around it.

2.q: What is the ledger, as Unit 2 describes it?
options: A simple list of the files in the project
A billing log of how much each run cost
The agent's own summary of what it did
A sealed record the system writes at a chokepoint
2.explain: The ledger is a tamper-evident record the system writes, not the agent, so you can trust what it says.

2.q: What does turning your review into an eval give you?
options: A reusable test a second AI grades automatically
A one-time check you run before shipping once
A manual checklist you re-read on each change
An extra deployment step in the release flow
2.explain: An eval is your review made reusable; a grader AI checks every change against your standard via the ledger.

3.q: What four standards make up a workbook bundle?
options: Code, config, logs, and data files
HTML face, SQLite disk, org why, one-line manifest
Frontend, backend, database, and an account
CSS, JavaScript, JSON, and image assets
3.explain: The bundle binds four standards: an HTML face, a SQLite disk, an org file, and a one-line manifest.

3.q: Which over-claim about workbooks does Unit 3 explicitly retire?
options: That a workbook opens in an ordinary browser
That a workbook can be emailed to someone
That a workbook needs no server at all
That a workbook is a single portable file
3.explain: No server is the over-claim; for the interesting things a workbook stands on a runtime.

options: A plain zip file openable with ordinary unzip
A proprietary, vendor-only archive format
An encrypted vault that needs a special key
A binary blob only the engine can read
3.explain: A .wbundle is just a zip with a familiar extension, openable by the unzip on every computer.

3.q: Where does a workbook keep its identity, so a rename can't break it?
options: In a magic byte at the start of the file
Registered in an entry on a remote server
In the file's name and its extension
In an inert marker block inside the file
3.explain: Identity rides in a self-describing block the browser won't run, so renaming the file can't knock it loose.

options: A roughly twenty-year-old open plain-text convention
A proprietary format this project invented
A brand-new format designed for AI agents
A database query language for tabular data
3.explain: Org is a long-standing open convention for notes, to-dos, and schedules, borrowed rather than invented here.

3.q: What trade does org refuse to make?
options: Choosing local storage or cloud storage
Holding prose or structure, but never both at once
Running for free or running for a fee
Optimizing for either speed or for safety
3.explain: Org keeps prose and structure together in one plain-text format, readable, writable, and checkable.

3.q: What does a workbook carrying its own story actually depend on?
options: The runtime staying connected at all times
An active subscription to a history service
Something recording intent and changes into the org layer
Nothing; file-ness provides it automatically
3.explain: The story travels only because you or an agent records it in the org layer; it's enabled by the format, not free.

4.q: Why is an ungranted power safer than a merely forbidden one?
options: Forbidden powers cost more to run than granted ones
Forbidden powers are encrypted and ungranted ones aren't
There is no real difference between the two
An ungranted power has no check to slip past
4.explain: A forbidden power relies on a check that can fail; an ungranted one has no path to call at all.

4.q: What is the Nexus in the system?
options: The engine, a place you set workbooks down on
A file you carry from one machine to another
A single agent that builds your workbook for you
A metering service that bills you per request
4.explain: The Nexus is the load-bearing engine you stand on, not a portable file or an agent or a meter.

4.q: Docking a workbook on the Nexus turns on which three properties?
options: Local, cloud, and mobile delivery
Isolated, stateful, and agentic
Fast, free, and fully private
Signed, compiled, and published
4.explain: Setting a file on the Nexus flips three lights: it becomes isolated, stateful, and agentic.

4.q: What one sentence do the sandbox and safe-powers lessons share?
options: Least privilege should always win out
Trust the agent but verify everything
Grant the verb, keep the noun
Encrypt every secret while it rests
4.explain: Both land on grant the verb (the ability) while keeping the noun (the dangerous key or credential).

4.q: What does the corrected minimal profile actually include?
options: Wide-open outbound network access
Disk only, fully sealed off from everything
Nothing at all; it's a pure dead scratch space
Disk, commands, KV, queue, plus secrets and sockets
4.explain: Minimal is not a sealed scratch space; it also grants secrets and brokered, revocable sockets per policy.

4.q: In going-live, how do you move a prototype to production?
options: Change one setting: where it runs
Rewrite the whole thing for the cloud
Assemble a committee of vendor approvals
Paste the production secrets into the config
4.explain: Local and cloud are two values of one where-it-runs setting; the same packaged engine runs both.

4.q: What does the public changes endpoint expose, and how?
options: The build tools, but only to admins
An anonymous, read-only feed of recent changes
The workbook's secrets, behind a login wall
Nothing; the route does not exist publicly
4.explain: A live workbook serves its recent history anonymously and read-only; dangerous routes don't exist on the public door.

4.q: Why can one ordinary machine carry many docked workbooks at once?
options: Each workbook gets its own virtual machine
Cloud autoscaling silently spins up more servers
The BEAM was built to juggle many tiny isolated processes
All the workbooks quietly share a single process
4.explain: Every docked workbook is a lightweight BEAM process, and juggling huge numbers of them is what that engine was made for.

5.q: What does a toolkit bundle into one object?
options: Code that runs, a safe place to run it, and a manual
A frontend, a backend, and a database
An author step, a build step, and a ship step
A model, a prompt, and a training dataset
5.explain: A toolkit ships the program, the sandbox-shaped place to run it, and the manual as one object.

5.q: What are a toolkit's three layers called?
options: The head, the body, and the tail
The manual, the muscle, and the floor
The top, the middle, and the base
The UI, the logic, and the data
5.explain: The three layers are the manual (words), the muscle (the program), and the floor (the sandbox).

5.q: Why can a toolkit's documentation never quietly drift out of date?
options: A team audits the docs every single night
The agent regenerates the docs on every run
The structured manual IS how the tool is reached
The documentation is kept strictly read-only
5.explain: The manual doubles as the agent's instructions, so there is no second hidden source to fall out of sync.

5.q: In code-in-the-document, where do component connections live?
options: Drawn by hand in a separate wiring diagram
Held inside each code block alongside the logic
Managed by an external orchestrator service
In short tags in the prose layer, matched by label
5.explain: Connections live as plain tags; a line appears where a produced label meets a consumed one, never by reading code.

5.q: What kind of error can validating a document catch before it builds?
options: A dangling input that nothing produces
A spelling mistake in the prose layer
A slow runtime once the system is live
A network outage during deployment
5.explain: The plan is testable: empty components and dangling inputs are named errors caught before anything compiles.

5.q: What is work, and who usually drives it?
options: An AI model that writes the code for you
A configuration file the engine reads at startup
A CLI for workbooks the agent usually drives
A web dashboard the user logs into directly
5.explain: work is the one command-line handle that authors, builds, signs, ships, and runs; you direct and the agent operates it.

5.q: How does work behave differently for people versus machines?
options: Same work; warm menus for people, clean codes for machines
It is two entirely separate programs underneath
It refuses any input that comes from a program
It always shows colored menus and never plain text
5.explain: One program changes only its manners: friendly for humans, machine-readable output and stable codes for programs.

5.q: By the founder's own admission, which prong is least mature?
options: The engine that runs everything
The sandbox the tools run inside
The work command-line tool
Toolkits, whose parts bin is small
5.explain: Toolkits are the youngest prong; the floor is solid but the collection grows one conversion at a time.

6.q: How many built-in tools does an agent get, and what is it?
options: Two: a shell and a web browser
Exactly one: a shell
Many, through installed plugins
None; it only produces words
6.explain: An agent gets one hand, a shell; every other capability arrives through toolkits with their own manuals.

6.q: What is the minimal definition of an agent?
options: A scheduled cron job that fires on a timer
An autonomous digital employee that thinks for itself
A model, in a loop, with tools
A chat window that remembers past messages
6.explain: An agent is a model, in a loop, with tools; the loop is the whole trick, nothing is hidden.

6.q: What four things does an agent need, like a human colleague?
options: A login, an email, a calendar, and a chat
Code, a sandbox, a manual, and a model
CPU, RAM, disk, and a GPU
Files, processes, memory, and time
6.explain: An agent needs files, processes, memory, and time, and pointedly NOT your operating system.

6.q: What makes a started run persistent, surviving you walking away?
options: Splitting request from work; you get a named receipt
Keeping the connection open the entire time
Running on a noticeably faster model
Pre-computing and caching the answer ahead of time
6.explain: Request and work are split; a receipt with the run's name returns in milliseconds while the worker grinds on.

6.q: In the persistence lesson, what is the receptionist's job?
options: To call the model and run all the tools
To decide when a run should be stopped
To stay reachable and answer status instantly
To pay the bills for the running work
6.explain: The receptionist stays reachable and answers status while the worker does the heavy labor; you never talk to the busy thing.

6.q: How do idle standing agents keep costs down?
options: They cache the model locally to avoid calls
They shut down permanently after one idle check
They wait to be poked and never wake on their own
They report no work and the system backs off
6.explain: On an idle wake-up the agent says no work; the gaps stretch, then snap back to a quick rhythm when real work returns.

6.q: What separates a real eval from just asking a model if the answer looks good?
options: It runs many more times to be sure
It uses a strict exact-string match
It relies on a much bigger judge model
The judge sees the path: steps, tools, and errors
6.explain: The judge grades the work via the logged path, telling a clean answer apart from a lucky, fumbling one.

7.q: What single concept runs the whole plan engine?
options: A scheduler config you switch on
Rules for assigning tasks to people
Readiness: unfinished, with dependencies done
Priority levels set on each task
7.explain: From readiness alone the order of work falls out; no sequence is drawn by hand.

7.q: How is parallelism expressed in a compiled plan?
options: By marking the relevant steps as urgent
By assigning steps to separate threads
By flipping a parallelism setting on
By the absence of a dependency between steps
7.explain: Parallelism is the absence of a dependency; unconnected steps land in the same layer and run together.

7.q: A workbook's kanban board is best described as what?
options: A two-way rendering of the one plan file
A separate database that stores the cards
A read-only screenshot of the plan
A cloud tracker synced to the project
7.explain: Drag a card to done and the word in the file flips; the board is the one plan file wearing different clothes.

7.q: What is the one-directional safety rule for changing a deployed plan?
options: What you give and what you demand may both grow freely
Gives may grow but never shrink; demands shrink, never grow
Any change at all is safe once a human signs off on it
Demands may grow freely, but what you give may not change
7.explain: Removing an output can break downstream readers; demanding more may exceed what a host grants.

7.q: What keeps a declared schedule honest, since a file can't fire itself?
options: The user manually triggers the run each time
A cloud cron service the file reaches out to call
An engine-side cadence heartbeat that wakes the agent
Nothing; it simply relies on good luck
7.explain: The declared time is read-only intent; an engine-side heartbeat is what actually shows up to honor it.

7.q: How does a step in a compiled plan receive its input?
options: From one shared global variable they all share
Every step reads the entire plan file each time
The user passes inputs by hand on each run
It looks up its feeder in a name-to-result list
7.explain: A running list maps each step's name to its result; the downstream step looks up its feeder and receives that result.

options: A monitoring dashboard that watches the running system
An agent on a maintenance plan editing the config layer
An automatic compiler that builds the whole system for you
A new kind of engine that rewrites its own source code
7.explain: The autopoet is an agent plus a plan pointed inward; it edits text config, never the fixed engine.

8.q: Why must a portable workbook's origin proof ride inside the file?
options: A separate proof re-attaches a string the file cut
Because a vouching server is too slow to check on demand
To save space compared to keeping an external record
To let the origin proof carry a built-in expiry date
8.explain: A separate .sig or a registry re-introduces a second file or a network dependency, defeating the portable-file point.

8.q: What is a signer's identity in a workbook signature?
options: A certificate authority's record of the signer
The public half of the keypair, written out in full
A plain email address tied to the account
A username that points to a key on a server
8.explain: The identity is the key itself, written out, so it's self-proving and verification needs nothing but the file.

8.q: What are the three sharing stances a workbook can declare?
options: Free, Trial, and Paid tiers
Local, Cloud, and Hybrid hosting
Public, Gated data, and Gated route
Open, Closed, and Locked modes
8.explain: The three honest stances are Public, Gated data, and Gated route, declared before the file is built.

8.q: When is a leak of a gated secret prevented?
options: At the moment the page first loads in the reader's browser
At build time; a gated workbook won't build for a public host
Only when the reader types in the correct password to unlock
Never; a leak can only be detected after it has happened
8.explain: The leaking file is simply never created, because a gated workbook can't be built for a host that hands it to anyone.

8.q: Where does the key to a sealed section live, and what is it?
options: Cleverly hidden somewhere inside the file itself
Stored on the reader's own device keychain
Baked identically into every copy of the file
At the runtime, decided fresh each time someone proves access
8.explain: The lock travels with the file; the key stays home at the runtime and is a live access decision, not a stored value.

8.q: What is the dead-man switch of runtime-held keys?
options: Deleting the one key makes every copy go dark at once
A timer that makes each file self-destruct
A remote wipe that erases all the copies
An automatic backup of every copy made
8.explain: Files stay put but stop meaning anything once the shared key is deleted; it's not a remote wipe.

8.q: What is a workbook's own disk, and what happens when you send the workbook?
options: The user's real disk, so nothing actually moves
A disk built on tables that travels inside the file
A cloud folder, so only a link gets sent along
A scratch folder that resets on each transfer
8.explain: The disk belongs to the project, not a machine; sending the workbook sends the disk exactly as it stood.

8.q: How does a workbook reach live outside data while keeping the seal tight?
options: By disabling the sandbox for the duration of the fetch
By the agent opening its own network connection
By pasting periodic exports into the file by hand
By naming an outside source the host fetches via an audited path
8.explain: The description names the source but never holds the key; the host fetches over one audited path and hands back rows, not credentials.

9.q: What is the kernel, and how many copies exist across surfaces?
options: A small Rust crate; one reader, the same everywhere
A large framework, with one copy per platform
An AI model that runs in the cloud
Three separate readers kept in coordination
9.explain: The kernel is one small reader, the same in browser, CLI, and server, so a tag means the same thing everywhere.

9.q: What does one program with no hands mean for the kernel's core?
options: It has no logging or error handling built into it
It can't open files, reach the network, or ask the time
It ships without any kind of user interface at all
It cannot be extended with new features later on
9.explain: Touching nothing, text in and text out, means the core has no opinion about where it runs.

9.q: Why does running everywhere here mean less code, not more?
options: Each platform quietly shares one central server
Unused features are stripped out at build time
The powerless core was never ported; one version, three doors
The whole crate is heavily compressed
9.explain: Normally everywhere means a version per place; here the tiny powerless core needs no per-place variant.

9.q: How can the renderer, planner, and safety gate be the same machine?
options: They were quietly merged together to save on space
They all just happen to run on the very same server
They simply read from one shared configuration file
One machine asked different questions about the text
9.explain: Read text, understand its structure, answer one question; a to-do list and a build plan are the same shape.

9.q: Where do new powers come from, since the reader stays powerless?
options: From toolkits, granted deliberately one at a time
From quietly enlarging the kernel over time
From the operating system underneath
From the renderer reaching outward
9.explain: Growth happens at the edges through granted toolkits, so the center stays small and trustworthy.

9.q: What is the honest today-versus-horizon framing in Unit 9?
options: Nothing actually ships yet; the whole thing is still planned
Kernel, seam, and toolkits ship; self-editing is being built
Everything, self-improvement included, fully ships today
Only the renderer ships; the rest is theory for now
9.explain: The kernel, the single seam, and toolkits are real and shipping; a system editing its own toolkits to improve is a direction in progress.
